tldr: By introducing a temporary "virtual downhill gravity" early in reinforcement learning, the robot discovers energy-efficient gaits that exploit its natural dynamics, cutting level-ground energy consumption by up to over 18%.
hero_caption: Overview of the proposed "slope-to-flat" curriculum. Early in training (Phase 1), a tilted gravity field assists forward progression, the tilt is gradually reduced (Phase 2), and the robot finally transitions back to nominal flat-ground dynamics (Phase 3).
overview:
When teaching humanoid robots to walk efficiently, conventional reinforcement learning typically relies on penalty rewards for torque or mechanical work. However, these only encourage the robot to "suppress excessive effort." They cannot directly guide the step-to-step mechanical energy transfer that dictates true walking efficiency. Furthermore, imitating human motion capture data does not necessarily lead to mechanical energy savings, because robots differ significantly from humans in actuator drives and the presence of elastic tendons.

To solve this, the authors drew inspiration from passive dynamic walking (PDW), where an unpowered walker moves down a shallow slope using only gravity. They devised a method that keeps the collision geometry completely flat in the simulator, but tilts the gravity vector acting on the robot in the direction of progression during early training, creating a virtual downhill slope. This assistance allows the robot to autonomously discover gait coordination that leverages gravity and body inertia. By pairing this with reward terms that selectively penalize wasteful positive actuator work (injecting energy) and decaying the gravity tilt to zero as training progresses, the robot transitions smoothly back to flat ground.

Evaluated on a 29-DoF Unitree G1 humanoid, the framework reduced the mechanical Cost of Transport (CoT) by 6.8 to 15.2% across speeds without sacrificing velocity tracking. Furthermore, when extended to omnidirectional locomotion and combined with an Adversarial Motion Prior (AMP), CoT improved by up to 18.7%, and these energy-saving benefits were confirmed on the physical robot.
contributions: Proposed a passive-dynamic-walking-inspired dynamics guidance framework that temporarily provides a tilted-gravity assist early in training and completely removes it before returning to nominal dynamics.

Demonstrated through detailed mechanical-work decomposition that earlier gait acquisition and converged energy economy are independent effects, and that reducing positive actuator work is the primary driver of efficiency gains.

Extended the curriculum to omnidirectional locomotion and combined it with a human motion prior (AMP), achieving super-additive energy savings and improved gait stability beyond what either provides alone.

sections.heading: Why is energy-efficient walking so hard for humanoids to learn?
sections.summary: Walking energy efficiency depends on distributing mechanical work across foot-strike transitions, but reinforcement learning objectives struggle to discover this coordination on their own. This paper proposes a framework that temporarily biases the early training dynamics toward passive-dynamic-friendly conditions, letting the robot spontaneously discover mechanically economical gaits suited to its body.
sections.details:
Human walking is remarkably energy-efficient because it smoothly transfers center-of-mass momentum from one step to the next, minimizing wasteful work. However, achieving this coordination through reinforcement learning (RL) faces major hurdles. Commonly used penalties on torque or work merely act to throttle output power. When tuned too high, they degrade velocity tracking and balance stability.

Imitation learning using human motion capture data (such as AMP) is also popular, but humans and robots have vastly different skeletal structures, joint configurations, and passive elastic tendons. Consequently, matching visual joint kinematics does not guarantee minimal mechanical actuator work.

This is where Passive Dynamic Walking (PDW) offers inspiration. On a shallow slope, passive dynamic walkers travel stably without any actuator power, relying solely on the interaction between gravity, inertia, and contact timing. The authors reasoned: "If we temporarily reproduce downhill-like mechanical conditions during early training, wouldn't the robot naturally discover an energy-efficient gait pattern tailored to its own physical dynamics?" Without requiring any reference trajectories, gait phases, or contact schedules, this study builds and evaluates a unique curriculum that temporarily tilts the training environment's gravity field.

captions.F1: Conceptual diagram of the proposed three-phase curriculum. Phase 1 introduces a tilted-gravity field assisting sagittal progression, Phase 2 gradually transitions back toward flat ground, and Phase 3 completely removes all assistance to optimize command-tracking under nominal flat-ground dynamics.

sections.heading: The intersection of passive dynamic mechanics and reinforcement learning
sections.summary: Prior research on energy-efficient walking either embedded passive dynamic principles into hardware or controllers, or focused on crafting RL rewards and regularizers. This work takes a previously unexplored approach: temporarily modifying the physics of the training environment itself during exploration.
sections.details:
### II-A Passive Dynamic Walking and Efficient Walking Mechanics
Passive dynamic walking originated with McGeer's seminal work, showing that limit-cycle walking can emerge without actuators by converting gravitational energy into forward propulsion. Later, "virtual slope" controllers were proposed to supplement slope-equivalent energy with actuators on flat ground. However, these require maintaining specific control laws on the physical robot during runtime, which becomes extremely difficult as degrees of freedom increase.

### II-B Reinforcement Learning for Legged Robots
Recent RL-based bipedal locomotion has advanced to the point of acquiring highly perturbation-resistant gaits without complex trajectory planning. While curriculum learning with external force assists has been used to scaffold skill acquisition, these acted primarily as "training wheels" to prevent falls and simplify exploration. None used structured assistance rooted in passive dynamic mechanics to fundamentally elevate the walking efficiency of the final policy.

### II-C Learning Energy-Efficient Gaits
Existing efforts to minimize energy consumption have mainly relied on torque or electrical power penalty rewards, or formulated efficiency as a constraint using Lagrangian methods (such as ECO). Others designed specialized 10-DoF robots tailored for passive walking. In contrast, the novelty of this method lies in improving the efficiency of a nominal flat-ground policy on unmodified robot hardware, simply by temporarily changing the energetic load conditions (the gravity field) during training.

sections.heading: Recreating a downhill slope on flat ground: how dynamics guidance works
sections.summary: While keeping the contact floor completely flat, the virtual gravity vector is tilted along the commanded heading to recreate downhill dynamics. Concurrently, reward terms penalizing positive work and rewarding a velocity tolerance band are phased in, and both the tilt and extra rewards decay to zero as training advances.
sections.details:
### III-A Task Formulation and Baseline Reward
The robot is a 29-DoF Unitree G1, tracking horizontal velocity commands $\mathbf{c}_{v,t}$ and a yaw rate command $\omega_{z,t}^{*}$. The baseline reward function $r_t^{\mathrm{base}}$ includes standard terms for velocity tracking, base stability, joint regularization, smoothness, and torque minimization, and is shared across all experiments.

### III-B Command-Responsive Tilted-Gravity Curriculum
The gravity tilt is scheduled based on training progress $k$. The maximum tilt angle $\theta_{\mathrm{init}}=5^{\circ}$ is held for $K_w$ episodes, then linearly decayed to $0^{\circ}$ over $K_t=200$ episodes. Crucially, rather than tilting the physical floor geometry, the gravity vector $\tilde{\mathbf{g}}_t$ applied to each link is tilted aligned with the commanded progression axis. For backward walking, it is restricted to $\theta_{\mathrm{back}}=3^{\circ}$, and lateral movement receives no tilt assist. Because the ground geometry stays flat, each parallel simulation instance can efficiently apply individual tilt angles independently.

### III-C Curriculum-Coupled PDW Rewards
Tilting gravity alone might allow the robot to ignore the assist and spin its motors aggressively. Thus, additional rewards are introduced that decay in lockstep with the tilted gravity:
- **Positive Mechanical Work Penalty $r_t^{\mathrm{PW}}$**: Only penalizes "positive work ($P_{j,t} > 0$)" where actuators inject energy, while leaving "negative work (energy absorption)" unrestricted for shock absorption and stabilization.
- **Velocity Band Reward $r_t^{\mathrm{VB}}$**: Gives a flat reward as long as the speed falls within a designated tolerance band rather than enforcing exact speed tracking, encouraging convergence to natural limit cycles characteristic of passive walking.
- **Both-Feet-Flight Penalty $r_t^{\mathrm{BF}}$**: Suppresses "bunny-hopping" gaits that frequently emerged during backward walking.

### III-D Extension to Omnidirectional Commands
Human lateral walking is not passive walking, but an extension of active side-to-side balance control. Hence, no lateral gravity assist is given. The curriculum restricts commands to sagittal headings within $\pm 45^{\circ}$ early in training, then expands the command space to full $360^{\circ}$ and turning as the gravity assist fades.

### III-E Walking-Specific AMP Integration
To supply human-like full-body coordination, an Adversarial Motion Prior (AMP) trained on 127 walking motions extracted from the AMASS dataset is incorporated. AMP remains active even after the gravity curriculum completes, preserving kinematic movement quality.

captions.F3: Progression of the translation heading range (green sectors) and yaw rate range (blue arcs) across curriculum stages. Initial training (left) is restricted to $\pm 45^{\circ}$ sagittally, transitions outward (middle), and fully opens to $360^{\circ}$ omnidirectional and full yaw commands (right) as the tilt fades.

sections.heading: Evaluation environment and experimental protocols: ensuring a fair comparison
sections.summary: Simulations were conducted in Isaac Lab on a 29-DoF Unitree G1. Mechanical Cost of Transport (CoT) serves as the primary metric, paired with work decomposition into positive and negative components and speed-matched binning to eliminate velocity tracking discrepancies.
sections.details:
### IV-A Robot and Simulation Details
The setup uses a Unitree G1 ($33.34$ kg mass) driven by PD position control at a $50$ Hz control loop ($\Delta t=0.02$ s). The environment runs 1024 parallel instances with 20-second episodes. The collision ground is always a flat cell.

### IV-B Policy Architecture and Training Pipeline
The policy network pairs a single-layer LSTM (256 units) taking the past 5 observation steps with an MLP, trained using PPO for 15,000 updates (roughly 368 million environment steps). As discussed in the Appendix, feedforward MLPs also reproduce the core efficiency gains.

### IV-C Evaluation Metrics and Definitions
All evaluations are conducted under nominal gravity on flat ground, with all gravity assists and extra rewards completely removed.
- **Mechanical Cost of Transport (CoT)**: $\mathrm{CoT} = \sum_{t}\sum_{j}|\tau_{j,t}\dot{q}_{j,t}|\Delta t / (mgd)$, a dimensionless metric of energy expenditure.
- **Work Decomposition**: Strictly decomposed as $\mathrm{CoT} = \mathrm{CoT}^{+} + \mathrm{CoT}^{-}$ to isolate where energy savings originate.
- **Speed-Matched Binning**: Because policies can realize slightly different actual speeds, making direct CoT comparisons unfair, gaits are binned by realized velocity to compute averaged metrics.

### IV-D Real-Robot Validation Procedure
Trained policies were deployed on a physical G1 for forward and lateral walking. Without relying on external motion capture, distance $d$ was calculated via forward kinematics in simulation using onboard IMU and joint encoder logs, gathering 38 steady-state walking trials totaling 258 meters.

sections.heading: Experimental results: was work reduced while tracking speed was maintained?
sections.summary: In forward walking, the proposed framework cut CoT by 6.8 to 15.2%, with the savings coming almost entirely from reduced positive work as intended. Combining it with AMP achieved an 18.7% speed-matched CoT reduction, and real-world experiments showed 16.3% forward and 17.0% lateral efficiency gains.
sections.details:
### V-A Forward-Locomotion Mechanics
Evaluated across five random seeds, the proposed method significantly reduced CoT compared to the baseline across all commanded speeds from 0.5 to 2.0 m/s (a 9.7% drop at 1.0 m/s, and a 15.2% drop at 2.0 m/s). Speed tracking error remained virtually identical to the baseline (around 0.088 m/s at 1.0 m/s), proving that the robot did not achieve efficiency by simply walking slower.

### V-B Work Decomposition Analysis
Decomposing the work revealed that nearly all CoT savings (approx. 100% at 1.0 m/s, and 88% at 2.0 m/s) stemmed from reductions in positive work ($\mathrm{CoT}^{+}$). Negative work (energy absorption) was preserved, meaning the robot reduced wasteful drive torque while retaining leg compliance.

### V-C Curriculum Sensitivity Analysis
- **Stepping Emergence**: Introducing the velocity band reward (VB) accelerated the emergence of stable stepping by roughly a factor of three. In contrast, tilted gravity itself did not speed up stepping acquisition, but rather improved the final mechanical efficiency of the converged gait.
- **Tilt Angle**: An initial tilt around $5^{\circ}$ was optimal; an excessive tilt ($8^{\circ}$) caused learning to collapse. Furthermore, keeping the tilt active permanently more than doubled the CoT, proving the critical importance of using the assist strictly as a temporary scaffold.

### V-D Combining Omnidirectional Locomotion and AMP
On omnidirectional tasks, the curriculum alone reduced CoT by 3.75%, while AMP alone yielded 11.67%. Combining both resulted in an 18.66% reduction, demonstrating a super-additive synergy. AMP alone suffered a high robot stuck rate of around 16%, but adding the proposed curriculum slashed this to 4.6%, drastically boosting gait reliability.

### V-E Hardware Experiments on the Humanoid
When deployed on the physical G1, the proposed method + AMP improved CoT by 16.3% in forward walking and 17.0% in lateral walking compared to baseline + AMP. Visually, while policies without AMP exhibited an unnatural crouched posture, adding AMP produced an upright, human-like gait with straighter knees.

captions.F7: Hardware comparison on the Unitree G1. (a) Single-stride gait snapshots of each policy. Policies with AMP show straighter knees and natural upright posture. (b) Relative CoT reduction over baseline. The combination with AMP (red) shows substantial efficiency gains in both forward and lateral walking.

sections.heading: Discussion: why dynamics guidance works, and what challenges remain
sections.summary: Tilted gravity reshapes early exploration dynamics without relying on fragile reward tuning, steering the policy into an energy-efficient basin of attraction. However, performance remains biased toward sagittal motion, and hardware limitations like the absence of passive elastic ankles were highlighted.
sections.details:
### VI-A What Dynamics Guidance Fundamentally Changes
Conventional reward engineering easily degrades into a tug-of-war between task tracking and energy penalties. In contrast, altering the early training physics helps the robot fall into the basin of attraction for passive limit-cycle walking. Crucially, tilted gravity contributed to the quality of the converged gait rather than early gait acquisition, providing a fresh perspective on curriculum design.

### VI-B Division of Labor with the Motion Prior (AMP)
Analyzing joint power profiles revealed that AMP primarily drove joint-level energy redistribution (shifting mechanical work away from the knees toward the hips and ankles), whereas the gravity curriculum uniformly lowered total positive work across the entire system. In short, AMP provides kinematic coordination, while dynamics guidance optimizes kinetic efficiency, forming an elegant division of roles.

### VI-C Real-World Deployment and Limitations
While physical deployment saw marked gains in forward and lateral walking, backward walking did not reproduce the simulation improvements. Backward walking is not a simple time-reversal of forward walking; joint power polarities invert, meaning sagittal-symmetric gravity assistance could not fully optimize it. Additionally, mechanical CoT does not account for motor Joule heating or gearbox friction, and testing has so far been limited to a single robot morphology.

sections.heading: Conclusion and future outlook: moving toward hardware-policy co-design
sections.summary: Passive-dynamic-inspired dynamics guidance proves to be a powerful framework for discovering energy-efficient humanoid gaits that exploit natural physical dynamics. Future work points toward co-designing robot hardware (such as springs and dampers) informed by learned joint-power profiles.
sections.details:
This study demonstrated that energy-efficient locomotion policies can be obtained purely by temporarily altering the environment's physics during training, without leaving any assistance mechanisms in place at runtime. Positive actuator work was slashed substantially without manually designing reference trajectories or contact schedules.

For researchers, the most compelling takeaway is the effectiveness of designing the physical conditions under which the RL agent explores body mechanics, rather than solely fine-tuning reward functions. Looking ahead, the authors propose leveraging these empirical joint power distributions to place and tune passive elastic elements (such as springs) in robot legs, bridging policy learning and hardware co-design.

sections.heading: Appendix: insights from network architecture and detailed gait data
sections.summary: The energy-saving benefits persist even when replacing the recurrent LSTM policy with a simple Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP). The appendix also provides direction-specific breakdown data and joint-by-joint work distribution details.
sections.details:
### Policy Architecture Verification (LSTM vs. MLP)
To confirm whether the efficiency gains depended on the LSTM's memory capacity, comparative experiments were run replacing both policy and value networks with a 3-layer MLP (512-256-128). In the base setup without AMP, the MLP still achieved a clear efficiency improvement with the proposed method (CoT: 0.576) over the baseline (CoT: 0.620), proving that dynamics guidance is architecture-agnostic. However, when combining with AMP, an LSTM was essential to capture temporal coordination; training failed to stabilize with an MLP.

### Breakdown of Joint-Level Mechanical Work
Examining positive work across the three primary sagittal joints (ankle pitch, knee, hip pitch) showed that adding AMP slashed the knee's share of positive work from roughly 30-34% down to 17-20%, redirecting the burden to the hips (approx. 68-72%) and ankles (approx. 11%). While the robot remains more hip-dominant than biological human walking (where ankles account for 40-50% and knees 14-17%), the data confirms that shifting the knee primarily into an energy-absorbing role brings the coordination pattern much closer to biological gaits.

takeaways: Providing a temporary virtual downhill gravity (around 5 degrees) early in reinforcement learning cuts flat-ground walking energy consumption by up to over 15% after returning to nominal physics.

Selectively penalizing positive mechanical work (injecting energy) rather than total torque or work achieves efficiency without hindering the negative work (shock absorption) needed for stabilization.
Dynamics guidance (altering physical conditions) and motion priors (imitating human data) are orthogonal; combining them yields super-additive efficiency and enhances gait stability.
It is critical to use the assist strictly as a temporary scaffold that decays completely to zero; leaving it active continuously produces the opposite, detrimental effect.
limitations: Validation is restricted to a single hardware platform, the 29-DoF Unitree G1, leaving generalizability across different morphologies and gear ratios unverified.
The gravity tilt schedule and initial angle (5 degrees) are fixed manual hyperparameters, lacking an online self-adaptation mechanism tuned to robot mass or geometry.
In backward walking, the simulation efficiency gains were not reproduced on hardware, revealing challenges with sagittal-asymmetric mechanics.
The evaluation metric, mechanical CoT, measures only raw mechanical motor output, omitting motor winding Joule heating and inverter or transmission losses.
